title: Bien-être et soutien psychologique des jeunes
text: La santé mentale des jeunes est devenue une priorité de santé publique. Ce rapport du Réseau Démo Santé Mentale décrit la situation du bien-être psychologique des jeunes en France et propose des mesures concrètes. Les enquêtes menées auprès de nos membres montrent une augmentation de l'anxiété, de l'isolement et de la fatigue chez les étudiants et les jeunes actifs. Le soutien psychologique existe, mais il est difficile d'accès: les délais pour obtenir un rendez-vous dépassent souvent un mois, les consultations sont coûteuses et les services de santé universitaires manquent de personnel. Dans les zones rurales, il n'y a parfois aucun professionnel à proximité. La stigmatisation reste forte et beaucoup de jeunes hésitent à demander de l'aide. Nous demandons des consultations psychologiques gratuites et sans condition pour toutes les personnes de moins de vingt-cinq ans, la présence d'au moins un psychologue dans chaque établissement d'enseignement supérieur et la formation de premiers secours en santé mentale pour les enseignants et le personnel administratif. Les lignes d'écoute doivent être ouvertes en soirée et le week-end. La prévention est essentielle. Il faut des campagnes d'information qui réduisent la stigmatisation, des espaces de rencontre accessibles et des activités sportives et culturelles à faible coût. Le bien-être des jeunes dépend aussi de leurs conditions de vie: logement, revenus et perspectives d'emploi. Investir dans le soutien psychologique, c'est investir dans la santé de toute la société.
summary: Le Réseau Démo Santé Mentale alerte sur le manque de soutien psychologique pour les jeunes. Il demande des consultations gratuites, des professionnels dans les établissements et la lutte contre la stigmatisation.

title: Civic education across universities
text: Universities teach professions, but do they teach citizenship? This study from Demo Campus Network reviews how higher education institutions in Europe prepare students for democratic life and finds large differences between universities, countries and disciplines. In some institutions civic education is a compulsory module with academic credit. In many others it is an optional course taken by a small group of students who are already interested, or a series of events with no link to the curriculum. Students in technical and scientific fields are the least likely to encounter questions of democracy, ethics or public debate during their studies. The study highlights good practice. Service learning, where students work with community organisations and reflect on the experience, strengthens both academic skills and a sense of responsibility. Debates, student parliaments and simulations of European institutions help students understand how decisions are made. Universities that include students in their governing bodies give them a practical lesson in participation. We recommend credit-bearing civic modules available in every discipline, funding for service learning, and training for academic staff who teach citizenship. Universities should publish what they offer and report participation figures. Academic freedom and institutional autonomy must be respected, but the mission of a university includes preparing graduates for democratic life. A graduate who can analyse a policy, listen to a different view and take part in public decisions is as valuable to society as one who has a degree in the subject of their choice.
summary: Demo Campus Network reviews how universities teach citizenship and democratic skills. It recommends credit-bearing civic modules, community service learning and student representation in governance.

title: Droits des jeunes et participation citoyenne
text: Les jeunes ont des droits, mais ils les connaissent mal et peuvent rarement les faire valoir. Ce document du Forum Démo des Droits étudie la participation des jeunes à la vie publique et formule des propositions pour renforcer leurs droits. Dans de nombreuses communes, les conseils de jeunes sont consultatifs et leurs avis ne sont pas suivis. Les jeunes qui ne sont ni étudiants ni salariés sont presque absents des espaces de participation. La politique de la jeunesse est décidée sans eux, et les procédures de consultation sont complexes et peu connues. Beaucoup de jeunes déclarent que leur voix ne compte pas, ce qui nourrit l'abstention et la défiance envers les institutions. Nous proposons d'abaisser l'âge du vote à seize ans pour les élections locales et européennes, de donner aux conseils de jeunes un budget et un pouvoir de décision sur une partie des dépenses locales, et d'inscrire dans la loi une obligation de consulter les jeunes sur les politiques qui les concernent. Les consultations doivent être accessibles aux jeunes en situation de handicap, aux jeunes ruraux et à ceux qui sont issus de milieux populaires. L'information est un droit. Un portail simple, en langage clair, devrait expliquer aux jeunes quels sont leurs droits, comment les défendre et à qui s'adresser. L'éducation à la citoyenneté dès l'école donnerait les outils nécessaires pour participer. Une démocratie qui écoute ses jeunes est une démocratie plus solide.
summary: Le Forum Démo des Droits examine les droits civiques des jeunes et leur participation. Il propose le vote à seize ans, des conseils de jeunes décisionnaires et un accès simple à l'information.

title: Éducation à la paix et prévention des conflits
text: La paix ne se limite pas à l'absence de guerre: elle se construit au quotidien, par l'éducation, le dialogue et la confiance. Ce document de l'Alliance Démo pour la Paix présente le rôle de l'éducation à la paix dans la prévention des conflits et la consolidation de la paix. Dans un contexte de tensions internationales et de montée des discours de haine, les écoles et les associations de jeunesse jouent un rôle de premier plan. Les programmes d'éducation à la paix enseignent la résolution des conflits, l'écoute, l'esprit critique face à la désinformation et la compréhension des autres cultures. Les études montrent que les jeunes formés à la médiation sont moins exposés aux violences et plus actifs dans leur communauté. Nous recommandons d'inclure l'éducation à la paix dans les programmes scolaires, de former les enseignants et les animateurs de jeunesse à la médiation et à la gestion des conflits, et de soutenir les échanges entre jeunes de régions en tension. Les programmes de coopération internationale devraient financer des projets de dialogue interculturel et de réconciliation. La sécurité des jeunes est aussi en jeu. Les jeunes sont souvent les premières victimes des conflits, mais ils sont rarement associés aux processus de paix. Nous demandons que les jeunes soient représentés dans les négociations et dans les dispositifs de prévention, conformément aux résolutions internationales sur les jeunes, la paix et la sécurité. Construire la paix demande du temps, des moyens et la confiance de ceux qui la vivront.
summary: L'Alliance Démo pour la Paix défend l'éducation à la paix comme outil de prévention des conflits. Elle propose des programmes scolaires, la formation à la médiation et des échanges entre jeunes de régions en tension.

title: Equal treatment and inclusion in schools and universities
text: Human rights do not stop at the school gate. This report by Demo Rights Forum collects evidence on discrimination in schools and universities across Europe and sets out what institutions must do to make education equal and inclusive. Students report discrimination on many grounds: ethnicity, religion, disability, gender and sexual orientation, and migration background. LGBTIQ+ students in particular describe harassment and a lack of recognition of their identity in forms, in classrooms and in student housing. Students with disabilities describe buildings, exams and digital tools that were not designed with them in mind. In many cases the person who experienced discrimination does not report it, because they do not know where to go or fear consequences. We recommend binding equality and diversity plans for every education institution, with measurable targets and public reporting. Staff should receive regular training on equality and non-discrimination. Each institution needs a safe and independent channel for complaints, with clear deadlines and protection against retaliation. Accessibility should be a condition for public funding, not an optional extra. Inclusion is also a matter of curriculum. History, literature and civics should reflect the diversity of society, and teaching materials should be reviewed for stereotypes. Student organisations that represent minority groups should receive funding and a seat in decision-making bodies. Equality is a legal duty and a democratic value. Education that excludes some students fails all of them.
summary: Demo Rights Forum documents discrimination in education based on gender identity, ethnicity, disability and migration background. It asks for binding equality rules, training for staff and safe reporting channels.

title: A fair green transition for young workers
text: The shift to a low-carbon economy will create millions of jobs, but climate justice means asking who gets them. This briefing from Demo Climate Coalition examines how the green transition affects young workers and what governments should do about it. Young people carry the longest burden of climate change, and they enter a labour market that is changing fast. Many green jobs are short contracts, internships or platform work with little protection. Others require skills that schools and universities do not yet teach. Without action, the transition will reproduce existing inequalities between regions, between income groups and between generations. We recommend three measures. First, funded retraining and apprenticeship schemes in regions that depend on fossil fuels, open to workers under thirty and designed with local youth groups. Second, minimum standards for green jobs, including fair pay for traineeships and a right to a written contract. Third, a seat for young people in national energy and climate planning bodies, so that sustainability policy reflects the interests of those who will live with its results. Environmental policy must also be fair in how its costs are shared. Carbon pricing without social support hits low-income households hardest. Public transport, building renovation grants and affordable renewable energy for young tenants should come before new taxes. Climate action is popular among young people, but trust is fragile. A transition that is seen to be fair will be accepted and defended; one that is seen as unfair will be rejected.
summary: Demo Climate Coalition calls for a green transition that does not leave young workers behind. It asks for funded retraining, protection from precarious green jobs and a voice for young people in climate planning.

title: Fondi europei: accesso per le piccole associazioni
text: I finanziamenti dell'Unione europea sono un'occasione importante per le associazioni, ma molte realtà piccole non riescono ad accedervi. Questo documento della Coalizione Demo Terzo Settore descrive gli ostacoli più frequenti e propone alcune riforme. I bandi europei sono scritti in un linguaggio tecnico e richiedono competenze di progettazione che le piccole associazioni non hanno al proprio interno. Il cofinanziamento obbliga a trovare risorse proprie prima di ricevere il contributo, e i pagamenti arrivano in ritardo. La rendicontazione richiede una grande quantità di documenti e un errore può portare alla restituzione di somme già spese. Per un'associazione con pochi volontari, il rischio è troppo alto. Proponiamo di semplificare le procedure con importi forfettari e costi standard, di prevedere una prima fase di candidatura breve e di anticipare almeno metà del contributo. Servono sportelli locali di assistenza, gestiti da enti pubblici o da reti di volontariato, che aiutino le associazioni a leggere i bandi e a costruire partenariati. Le amministrazioni nazionali dovrebbero pubblicare in italiano guide chiare sui programmi europei e sulle scadenze. Riteniamo che la governance dei fondi debba includere la società civile fin dalla fase di programmazione. Le associazioni conoscono i bisogni dei territori e possono segnalare presto dove le regole non funzionano. Un sistema di finanziamento accessibile rafforza la partecipazione e la fiducia nelle istituzioni europee.
summary: La Coalizione Demo Terzo Settore spiega perché le piccole associazioni italiane faticano ad accedere ai fondi europei. Propone procedure semplificate, importi forfettari e assistenza locale.

title: Making exchange programmes reachable for everyone
text: Student mobility is one of the most visible successes of European cooperation, and the Erasmus programme has become a symbol of it. But who actually goes abroad? This report from Demo Mobility Alliance reviews participation in international exchange and study abroad schemes and finds that students from lower-income families, students with disabilities and vocational learners are still under-represented. The main obstacle is money. Monthly grants rarely cover the real cost of living in expensive host cities, and payment often arrives after the student has already paid a deposit for housing. Students who cannot rely on their family to cover the gap simply do not apply. Housing is the second barrier: rents near universities have risen faster than grants, and short stays make it hard to rent on the regular market. Information is a third problem. Students who are the first in their family to attend university often do not know that exchange is an option or how to apply. Language preparation is available mostly to those who already speak the host language. We recommend higher and country-adjusted grants, payment of at least eighty percent of the grant before departure, a guaranteed place in host-university housing for exchange students, and dedicated mobility schemes for vocational education and training. Universities should appoint an advisor for students with fewer opportunities and report on who takes part. International exchange should not be a privilege of those who can afford it. It should be a normal part of study for anyone who wants it.
summary: Demo Mobility Alliance finds that Erasmus-style exchanges still favour students from wealthier families. It proposes higher grants, upfront payment, housing support and mobility for vocational learners.

title: Mobilità studentesca: borse di studio e alloggi
text: Studiare all'estero con il programma Erasmus è un'esperienza che cambia la vita, ma in Italia non tutti possono permettersela. Questo documento della Rete Demo Studenti esamina gli ostacoli economici e organizzativi alla mobilità studentesca internazionale. La borsa di mobilità copre solo una parte dei costi, soprattutto nelle città europee dove l'affitto è molto alto. Il pagamento arriva spesso dopo la partenza, e le famiglie devono anticipare cauzioni e spese iniziali. Gli studenti con un reddito basso rinunciano più spesso, e così la mobilità rischia di diventare un'opportunità per pochi. Anche la ricerca di un alloggio è un problema: le università ospitanti hanno pochi posti nelle residenze e molti studenti si affidano a offerte private poco sicure. C'è poi un problema di informazione. Molti studenti non conoscono le scadenze, non sanno come funziona il riconoscimento dei crediti e temono di rallentare il percorso di studi. Le segreterie hanno poco personale per seguire le richieste. Chiediamo borse più alte e adeguate al costo della vita nella città di destinazione, un anticipo di almeno l'ottanta per cento prima della partenza, posti garantiti nelle residenze universitarie e un ufficio mobilità con personale dedicato in ogni ateneo. Il riconoscimento dei crediti deve essere concordato prima della partenza e rispettato al ritorno. Lo scambio internazionale deve diventare una parte normale del percorso universitario, aperta a tutte e tutti.
summary: Rete Demo Studenti analizza gli ostacoli economici alla mobilità Erasmus in Italia. Chiede borse più alte, anticipo del pagamento, alloggi garantiti e un'informazione più chiara.

title: Salute mentale e benessere nelle università
text: La salute mentale degli studenti è una questione di diritti e di qualità dell'istruzione. Questo rapporto della Rete Demo Studenti raccoglie le esperienze di studentesse e studenti universitari in diverse città italiane e descrive che cosa servirebbe per migliorare il benessere nelle università. Molti studenti dichiarano di sentirsi sotto pressione per gli esami, per i costi dello studio e per l'incertezza sul futuro. Il supporto psicologico esiste in quasi tutti gli atenei, ma i tempi di attesa sono spesso di diverse settimane e il numero di colloqui gratuiti è limitato. Chi vive lontano da casa, chi lavora durante gli studi e chi ha una disabilità incontra ostacoli ancora maggiori. Parlare di disagio psicologico è ancora difficile, e molti ragazzi non sanno a chi rivolgersi. Proponiamo di istituire in ogni università uno sportello di ascolto gratuito, con un numero di psicologi proporzionato agli iscritti e un tempo massimo di attesa di due settimane. Il personale docente e amministrativo dovrebbe ricevere una formazione di base per riconoscere i segnali di difficoltà e indirizzare gli studenti. Le università dovrebbero rivedere il calendario degli esami per ridurre lo stress e permettere sessioni più flessibili. Serve anche prevenzione: campagne contro lo stigma, attività sportive e culturali accessibili, spazi di socialità. Il benessere psicologico degli studenti non è un lusso, ma una condizione per studiare bene.
summary: Rete Demo Studenti segnala tempi di attesa lunghi per il supporto psicologico universitario. Propone sportelli gratuiti, più psicologi, formazione del personale e attenzione allo stress da esami.

title: Simpler funding for small organisations
text: EU funding is meant to support civil society in all its diversity, but in practice the biggest grants go to the biggest organisations. This paper from Demo Youth Network explains why small organisations struggle to access European funding and how the system could change. Applications are long and written in a technical style that often requires a paid consultant. Co-financing rules oblige an organisation to find part of the money elsewhere before it can receive any, and payments arrive late, so small groups must carry the cost for months. Reporting rules ask for detailed proof of every expense, which takes staff time that small teams do not have. Mistakes in these reports can lead to repayment demands that threaten the survival of the organisation. We propose five reforms. Use lump sums and simplified cost options wherever possible. Offer a short first-stage application so that organisations do not write a full proposal that fails. Pay at least half of the grant in advance. Create a single contact point at each institution that answers questions in plain language. Fund core costs, not only projects, so that organisations can keep their staff between grants. Governance matters too. Civil society should be part of the design of funding programmes, not only a recipient. Regular dialogue with the European institutions would show early where rules do not work. A funding system that excludes small organisations loses the local knowledge and trust that make European policy credible.
summary: Demo Youth Network shows that complex EU funding rules keep small organisations out of grants. It proposes simpler applications, lump sums, faster payment and a single contact point at the institutions.

title: Mental health support for students and young people
text: Young people increasingly say that stress, anxiety and loneliness affect their studies and their lives. This briefing from Demo Student Wellbeing Group summarises what students told us about mental health and wellbeing, and what universities and governments should do. In our survey, most students reported feeling under pressure because of exams, the cost of living and uncertainty about work. Counselling services exist, but waiting times of several weeks are common, and the number of free sessions is limited. Students who live far from home, who work while studying or who have a disability face the biggest barriers. Many do not ask for psychological support because they fear stigma or do not know where to go. We recommend that every university offers free and confidential counselling, with enough psychologists for the number of students and a maximum waiting time of two weeks. Teachers and administrative staff should receive basic training to recognise signs of distress and refer students to help. Exam calendars should be reviewed to reduce stress, with more flexible sessions and clear rules for students who fall ill. Prevention matters as much as treatment. Campaigns against stigma, affordable sport and cultural activities, and places where students can meet outside lessons all support wellbeing. Peer support schemes, run by trained students, can reach those who would never book an appointment. Mental health support is not a luxury. It is a condition for learning, and a public responsibility.
summary: Demo Student Wellbeing Group reports long waits for counselling and asks for free, quick mental health support in universities and youth services. It also proposes staff training and less exam pressure.

title: Youth voices in EU decision-making
text: Young people make up a large share of the European population, yet their voices rarely shape the decisions that affect them. This position paper from Demo Youth Network looks at how youth participation works in practice in European policy making and where it falls short. Our members report three recurring problems. First, consultations open late, often when the main choices have already been made. Second, the language of consultation documents is technical, which excludes young people who are not already part of policy circles. Third, there is almost never feedback: participants do not learn what happened to their input. We recommend a standing youth panel attached to each major policy file, with a fixed seat for representatives of youth organisations and a random selection of young citizens. Consultations should run for at least twelve weeks, be published in plain language and be open in all official languages. Every institution that consults young people should publish a short response explaining which proposals were taken up, which were not, and why. Youth rights are also at stake. Voting at sixteen in European elections, protection from discrimination in internships and access to information about their rights are all questions where young people should be heard first. A youth policy that is made for young people rather than with them will not hold. Finally, participation needs resources. Travel costs, interpretation and staff time should be covered so that small youth organisations, and not only large ones, can take part. Without this, participation stays a privilege.
summary: Demo Youth Network argues that young people are still consulted too late and too rarely on EU policy. It proposes a standing youth panel, plain-language consultations and feedback on how input was used.
